home.name: Louis Cagnion
home.pitch: Developer at Groupe Tressol-Chabrier, trained at 42 Perpignan. Starting from scratch in 2024, I build applications and data pipelines running in production.

entries.label: Education
entries.html: My name is Louis Cagnion and I am a student at 42 Perpignan. During my common core curriculum, I completed various projects that allowed me to learn C and C++, as well as several practical tools such as MinilibX for graphical rendering, Docker for sharing applications compatible with most environments, and how networks and APIs work. I also learned to manage data on a website visited by users through backend and frontend development.

entries.label: Current training
entries.html: Alongside my job, I practice in areas I have not yet had the chance to explore in depth, such as Python applied to AI, the use of LLMs, and the various tools used in data science, machine learning, and deep learning.

entries.label: Passion projects
entries.html: I also enjoy working on passion projects that broaden my knowledge and skills, such as this portfolio, through which I am learning frontend development with HTML, JavaScript, and CSS.

stops.title: First piscine
paragraphs: I humbly started coding during my first piscine at 42. Yes, I knew absolutely nothing about this world before starting the school's selection process. I did not even know what a terminal or an IDE was.

Someone told me about the school, their approach to learning programming, and the possible career paths after the core curriculum: it sounded interesting. So I tried the 42 piscine to see what I was capable of in this new environment.
As it turned out, I discovered a genuine passion during that selection process, even though starting from scratch was not easy.

One moment stood out in particular. At first, I was asking for help on the early exercises from people who already had programming experience. Then, when we moved on to C for most of the piscine, they were the ones coming to me for help because I had progressed further than them.

That was when I realised I might have potential in this field and, more importantly, that I genuinely loved practicing and improving. And yes, for those wondering, I helped them gladly. People had helped me get started, so it felt natural to give back.

Unfortunately, I did not pass my first piscine on the first try, even though my results were around the average of other candidates. I was disappointed, almost sad, but I went home with a new goal: try again and get into the school.

stops.title: Second chance
paragraphs: I was ready to prepare on my own for the next attempt, but fate had other plans. A few days after the results, I received a message from the school's director inviting me to join the next piscine, which was only three weeks away, whereas normally you have to wait a full year before retrying.
Obviously, I did not hesitate for a second. I eagerly accepted and was extremely happy to be back on the battlefield so quickly.

The beginning was tough, as I had to finish my notice period in the restaurant industry during the first days of this new piscine. Despite that, I managed to prepare in time for the first-week exam, got the maximum grade, caught up on everything over the weekend, and took part in the group project that was only unlocked during piscine weekends.

After giving everything I had during that second piscine, I was finally accepted, to my greatest joy and relief. I began my programming journey in November 2024, at the start of the school year for 42 Perpignan students.

stops.title: Common core
paragraphs: We theoretically had three years ahead of us to complete the core curriculum. For my part, I wanted to throw myself fully into learning to code. I chose to challenge myself by completing every possible bonus on the projects I picked.
I also wanted to move quickly while maintaining quality work, because going fast without actually learning anything would have been pointless. That is what I tried to do throughout my studies.

Even if I was not as fast as some friends I met during my piscines who finished the curriculum in six months, I still managed to complete all core curriculum projects in a year and a half, with bonuses whenever possible.

stops.title: Codewars
paragraphs: I also took the opportunity to try different learning tools by joining school events, particularly Coding Games. Personally, I did not really enjoy the format of that site, and someone told me about another platform better suited to what I was looking for.
That site is called Codewars (My profile). It offers a level, ranking, and experience system, while also letting you view community solutions once you finish an exercise.

Through that platform, I discovered many ways to solve problems in C, C++, and Python, as well as tools I had no idea existed. I was often impressed by how some developers could solve complex problems with short, elegant solutions.
It was also there, after learning the basics through tutorials, that I truly started developing my Python skills.

stops.title: Tressol-Chabrier
paragraphs: I focus on projects I consider useful, either to advance toward my future programming goals, or because they can bring something valuable to others or to myself.

Once I completed my common core, I joined the Groupe Tressol-Chabrier headquarters in Montpellier as a full-time developer. There, I took part in the design of internal applications (data search, dashboards, admin back-office), working on both the frontend and backend, which let me put my skills into practice in real-world conditions.
You can find the projects I have worked on in the "My projects" section.

stops.title: RNCP 6 work-study
paragraphs: With my common core completed, I joined the Groupe Tressol-Chabrier headquarters in Montpellier full-time on July 13, 2026. There, I started a two-year work-study program in September 2026 for the RNCP6 title of Software Solutions Designer and Developer (Concepteur développeur de solutions informatiques).

stops.title: RNCP 7 in AI
paragraphs: My underlying goal has not changed: once I complete this RNCP6, I plan to pursue a further one-year work-study program to earn an RNCP7 in AI and algorithmics. So I want to deepen my knowledge in the areas related to both qualifications, starting with software development, then AI and algorithmics for what comes next.

stops.title: AI research
paragraphs: In the longer term, my ambition is to contribute to AI research, with the goal of taking part in the advances toward artificial general intelligence (AGI), and beyond.

systems.name: Tressol-Chabrier
systems.intro: At the Groupe Tressol-Chabrier headquarters, I took part in developing several internal applications and data pipelines. For confidentiality reasons, I stay deliberately general about the business logic here and only describe the technical side of the code. These projects were built with the assistance of Claude Code: I designed, directed, reviewed and tested every change.

projects.title: A conversational search tool
projects.summary: Query the group's vehicle stock in natural language, thanks to an LLM that builds the Elasticsearch query.

blocks.html: I took over the development of a conversational search tool, started by a colleague, that lets users query the group's vehicle stock in natural language. A user query is first interpreted by an LLM, which extracts search criteria and rewrites it, before an Elasticsearch query is built accordingly.

On this project, I built a signed HMAC token authentication system that automatically resolves context (dealership, data source) without any manual per-dealership setup. I also fixed several data-quality bugs (encoding issues, empty fields, overly permissive brand/vehicle-type filters).

On the performance side, I cut a loading screen's payload from over 5 MB down to under 10 KB, re-enabled browser caching, and brought a critical endpoint's response time down from over a second to under 50 milliseconds.

The application is designed to serve several dealerships: the dealership identifier is set server-side when the token is validated and then injected into every request, so the client cannot alter it. I also added per-IP rate limiting and CSRF protection on requests that modify data. A crash-test campaign let me identify and fix about thirty bugs and vulnerabilities.

projects.title: Reporting dashboards
projects.summary: Internal dashboards to visualise and filter business data per dealership, including a management dashboard.

blocks.html: I contributed to several internal dashboards that let users visualise and filter business data per dealership (used-vehicle sales, quality, stock tracking), with a Power BI integration on one of them.
I notably worked on reworking the interface (filters, sidebar, layout) to make it usable on both desktop and mobile.

I also built a management dashboard covering several domains (new and used vehicle sales, calls, NPS, quality, events). It relies on 17 API endpoints and ECharts charts, and offers a network map whose addresses are batch-geocoded and cached. An atomic-write file cache keeps serving the last known state when the database is temporarily unavailable. It lets users select several dealerships at once and also covers the call centre and quality.

projects.title: NPS scores, from data to screen
projects.summary: From the quarterly workbook to the dashboard: a three-layer pipeline and a back-office module.

blocks.html: I built the daily pipeline that feeds NPS scores (new vehicles and after-sales) per dealership. It starts from a quarterly Google Sheets workbook and ends in a fact table consumed by Power BI, across three layers (Staging, Silver, Gold) on SQL Server, within the group's data platform.

The pipeline normalises brands, detects column shifts in the source workbook, matches each dealership to the group's reference data and merges the different spellings of the same town. Each layer is validated by a SQL consistency test (for example, an NPS score must stay between -100 and 100), and deployment goes through Azure Pipelines with a scheduled daily run.

On the back-office side, I also built the PHP module that displays these scores by quarter, brand and site, with a calculator to simulate targets. Data access is resilient: if the data warehouse is unavailable, the module falls back to a staging copy, then to a static JSON file, rather than crashing, and a file cache limits the number of queries.

projects.title: A nightly audit of online shops
projects.summary: A Python pipeline that checks every night how visible the group's online shops are on classified-ad platforms.

blocks.html: I built a Python pipeline that checks every night that the group's used-vehicle shops are properly visible on several classified-ad platforms. It counts the ads actually displayed, detects duplicate vehicles and measures the gap with the reference stock. Extraction relies on Playwright, in parallel per platform, handling cookie banners and anti-bot checks.

The pipeline deliberately stops when a shop displays no ads or when a duplicate is confirmed, and ends "with warnings" if some shops could not be read. It is deployed through Azure Pipelines (validation with Ruff and pytest, pre-production and production environments) and covered by several hundred tests.

Results can be browsed in a back-office module that I also built: a table that can be filtered and sorted by shop and platform, CSV export, "priority actions" cards and a dedicated alert for unread shops, including the cause of the failure.

projects.title: A PDF commercial-policy parser
projects.summary: Convert manufacturers' commercial-policy PDFs into structured JSON, versioned per brand.

blocks.html: I built a Python tool that converts manufacturers' commercial-policy PDFs into structured JSON, versioned per brand (titles, text, bullet lists and tables with typed cells: date, percentage, amount, integer). It is designed to feed a downstream chatbot.

Table detection works as a cascade: the PDF's native text first, a cross-check with img2table when a cell looks suspicious, then an OCR fallback (PaddleOCR) only if nothing was found. Doubtful values are flagged as "suspect" rather than silently passed through.

On the performance side, I cut processing time by about 30% by lowering the rendering resolution, and parallelised the OCR fallback according to available memory. The tool is covered by about 170 tests and has been proven on around twenty documents spanning more than ten brands.

projects.title: An admin back-office
projects.summary: NPS score, audit and call-tracking modules in the back-office shared across several internal applications.

blocks.html: I developed modules in the admin back-office shared across several internal applications: PHP 8 with Slim 4, SQL Server via PDO, one database per module and access rights per module and per profile.
I built the NPS score and online-shop audit modules described above in it, and I reworked the call-tracking module.

projects.title: Call resolution
projects.summary: Port the call centre's call resolution tool into the back-office, prototyped by a colleague in Python with Streamlit.

blocks.html: I ported the call centre's call resolution tool into the back-office; a colleague had prototyped it in Python with Streamlit. The module reads the data warehouse, lets users match each call to the right dealership and computes call billing, across six tabs designed to be usable without technical jargon, even on a phone. It is covered by 151 tests, 38 of them integration tests.

projects.title: A customer record migration
projects.summary: Prepare and send more than 430,000 customer records from an old software to the new one's API.

blocks.html: I wrote the Python scripts that prepared and then sent more than 430,000 customer records from an old software to the new one's API, in batches, with a resume point, sending logs and a report of the rejected records.

projects.title: An AI chatbot

blocks.html: In terms of AI, I created a chatbot that talks to a Mistral model run locally by Ollama: a JavaScript web interface and a small Express server that relays the messages, with no external API at all. I also ran experiments in a dedicated repository: data statistics and standardisation with NumPy, image processing, charts with Matplotlib and a first neural network with Keras.

projects.title: A full video game wiki
projects.summary: An interactive wiki around the game Heartopia: map, progress tracking and recipes with a profit calculator.

blocks.html: Using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, the same tools that let me share my story through this portfolio, I created an interactive wiki around the game Heartopia: a map to locate collectibles and wildlife, track progress and browse recipes, with a profit calculator.

Through this project, I want to help the French-speaking community, as well as myself, to better understand the game's mechanics, find resources, unlock certain achievements, and progress more easily.
My goal is to offer comparisons, observations, and various tips to simplify players' lives in a game with an enormous number of hidden mechanics and systems.
An admin panel makes it possible to edit the data directly from the browser. The project was developed with the assistance of Claude Code and is covered by unit tests.

projects.title: Devpedia, a software development encyclopedia
projects.summary: A software development encyclopedia, rendered by a hand-written Markdown parser and translated into three languages.

blocks.html: Devpedia is a website I created to document, explain, and share my knowledge of various software development topics. This project helps me deepen my understanding through research and teaching, practice building modern web interfaces, and make this knowledge accessible to anyone interested in learning.

The site covers several programming languages (C, C++, PHP, Python with data science and AI: NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, scikit-learn, neural networks, PyTorch, NLP and LLMs, as well as JavaScript), markup languages (HTML, CSS), domain-specific languages such as Regex and SQL, several shells (Bash, PowerShell, Zsh), and Git, from everyday use to its internal object model.

I wrote the foundations of the site, including the Markdown parser that renders each chapter, and I had integrated the DeepL API to translate each page automatically. Its free quota of one million characters did not last long, so I handed over to Claude Code, which wrote most of the content, added the new features and translated every page into English, Spanish and Portuguese. Each page can also be listened to, thanks to audio narration generated in all four languages.

projects.title: A grocery comparator

blocks.html: A web app that compares prices across several supermarkets, normalised to price per kilo or litre so that package sizes do not fool you. It generates the shopping list store by store while limiting the number of stops, accepts a list pasted from a notes app, and runs entirely in the browser. Developed with the assistance of Claude Code, with every change reviewed and directed by me, and covered by unit tests.

projects.title: Creativity box

blocks.html: My experiment box, where I allow myself anything, especially the most complicated way: three variants of printf recoded from scratch (fprintf, sprintf, asprintf), a solar system modelled in object-oriented C++ that ranks planets by mass, diameter, temperature or gravity, and a few everyday utilities, such as an RGB to Pantone colour converter or a workout tracker.

systems.name: 42 Perpignan
systems.intro: During my studies, I had the opportunity to work on several particularly interesting solo and group projects.

projects.title: Libft
projects.summary: Recreate about forty functions of the C standard library, then linked lists as a bonus.

blocks.html: The very first project of the curriculum: recreate about forty functions of the C standard library (string and memory handling, conversions, output), then, as a bonus, a small linked-list toolbox. This library then followed me through all my C projects, to the point of becoming the Ultimate libft.

projects.title: Ft_printf
projects.summary: Recreate the printf function and its formatting options.

blocks.html: Recreate the printf function with the conversions c, s, p, d, i, u, x, X and %. The bonuses added the formatting options: width, precision and the flags -, 0, ., #, + and space, all of whose combinations must behave exactly like the original.

projects.title: Get_next_line
projects.summary: A function that returns a file line by line, whatever the size of the read buffer.

blocks.html: Write a function that returns a file line by line, whatever the size of the read buffer chosen at compile time, with no memory leaks. The bonus required reading several files at the same time without mixing up their lines.

projects.title: Born2beroot
projects.summary: My first server: a Debian virtual machine installed and hardened by hand.

blocks.html: My first server: a Debian virtual machine installed and hardened by hand, with encrypted partitions under LVM, SSH on a dedicated port, a UFW firewall, a strict password policy, sudo logging and a monitoring script run every ten minutes by cron. As a bonus, I added a WordPress site served by lighttpd with MariaDB and PHP, as well as an extra service of my choice.

projects.title: Push_swap
projects.summary: Sort a random list of 500 integers in fewer than 5500 operations, with two stacks and very limited moves.

blocks.html: The goal of this project was to write the most efficient sorting algorithm possible to sort up to 500 numbers.
To get the maximum grade, you had to sort a random list of 500 integers in fewer than 5500 operations using very limited moves.
In short: imagine two stacks, the second one empty, and you can only interact with the top or bottom element of each stack to move numbers around.

I managed to develop an algorithm that sorted in around 5700 moves on average. I was proud of the method I found after testing several different approaches, even though I eventually had to draw inspiration from an existing algorithm to get under 5500 operations.
The bonus was to create a "Checker" to verify that a sequence of operations resulted in a correctly sorted list at the end.

projects.title: Pipex
projects.summary: Reproduce in C a chain of commands connected by pipes, with fork, pipe, dup2 and execve.

blocks.html: Reproduce in C the behaviour of < file cmd1 | cmd2 > file with fork, pipe, dup2 and execve. The bonuses added any number of chained commands and here_doc, which reads the input until a limiter word and appends to the output file.

projects.title: Minitalk
projects.summary: Make a client and a server talk using only two signals, SIGUSR1 and SIGUSR2.

blocks.html: Make a client and a server talk using only two signals, SIGUSR1 and SIGUSR2: each character is sent bit by bit, and the server acknowledges each one, so none gets lost on the way.

projects.title: Fract-ol
projects.summary: A graphical rendering of fractals with MinilibX.

blocks.html: This project was more artistic. The goal was to use MinilibX to create a graphical rendering of fractals.
For those unfamiliar with fractals: they are patterns that repeat infinitely as you zoom in. Romanesco broccoli is a great example of a natural fractal.
The bonuses consisted of:

items: Creating a third fractal, Multibrot, in addition to Julia and Mandelbrot
Making the zoom follow the mouse position
Moving the camera with arrow keys
Dynamically changing the fractal's colours

projects.title: Minishell
projects.summary: Recreate a shell as a group; I wrote the pipes, some builtins and the logical operators with their priorities.

blocks.html: The goal of this first group project was to recreate a mini shell (no way !).
Requirements included:

items: Navigating different shell levels
Recreating several Bash commands such as cd, echo, pwd, export, and exit
Managing history
Implementing redirections (<, >, <<, >>)
Handling environment variables
Handling keyboard signals like Ctrl+C, Ctrl+D and Ctrl+\

blocks.html: The bonuses involved adding the logical operators '&&' and '||', priority management using parentheses and the wildcards '*'.
For my part, I wrote the pipes, the cd, env, exit and pwd builtins, and the whole bonus part on logical operators and priorities: a binary tree that carries the execution order of the commands.

projects.title: Philosophers
projects.summary: Keep philosophers alive to the millisecond, with threads and mutexes.

blocks.html: In this project, the goal was to keep philosophers alive.
Each philosopher had several states:

items: A time to eat
A time to think
A time to sleep
A number of meals to reach (optional)

blocks.html: They also had a limited lifespan. The goal was to provide different time parameters and varying numbers of philosophers, then be precise enough to keep them alive given the constraints.
Times were expressed in milliseconds, so the slightest miscalibration was immediately noticeable.
On top of that, you had to display precisely when each philosopher performed an action, with an error margin of less than 10 ms.

The catch was that philosophers could only eat if two forks were available. However, each philosopher only owned one fork. So you had to properly organise access to avoid deadlocks, conflicts, and premature deaths.
The bonuses consisted of redoing the same exercise by replacing threads with child processes and mutexes with semaphores.

projects.title: Netpractice
projects.summary: Ten levels of small networks to configure: IP addresses, subnet masks, gateways and routing.

blocks.html: Ten levels of small networks to get working: IP addresses, subnet masks, gateways and routing tables, without a single line of code but with a lot of binary calculation.

projects.title: Cub3D
projects.summary: A game inspired by Wolfenstein 3D, with a raycasting engine; I wrote the map parser, the collisions, the minimap and the movement.

blocks.html: The goal of this second group project was to create a game inspired by Wolfenstein 3D, with a raycasting engine: a two-dimensional map projected in pseudo-3D.

For my part, I wrote the map parser, the collision with walls, the minimap, as well as the character's movement and speed handling. My partner took care of the raycasting, the wall textures, the entities and the bonus up-and-down view.
The bonuses included:

items: Adding collision detection
Implementing a minimap
Adding doors
Creating animated sprites
Handling camera movement with the mouse

blocks.html: The person I worked with on this project even added a vertical camera, although raycasting only projects a two-dimensional map, with no looking up or down.
He was also remarkable throughout the project: even when I was less available, he kept pushing things forward on his own. That definitely deserves recognition.

projects.title: The C++ modules
projects.summary: Ten modules to go from C to object-oriented C++ (C++98), from classes to templates and the STL.

blocks.html: Ten modules to go from C to object-oriented C++ (C++98):

items: Classes and first steps (00), memory, references and pointers to members (01)
Canonical form and operator overloading with a fixed-point number (02)

projects.title: Inception
projects.summary: Create your own Dockerfiles and docker-compose with Nginx, MariaDB and WordPress, inside a virtual machine.

blocks.html: In this project, the task was to create our own Dockerfiles and docker-compose using Nginx, MariaDB, and WordPress.
The container had to be created and run inside a virtual machine.
The bonuses included:

items: Adding a Redis cache to WordPress
Setting up an FTP server pointing to the WordPress volume
Creating a static website without PHP
Configuring Adminer
Adding an extra service deemed useful

blocks.html: This is probably the project I enjoyed the least and the one I struggled with the most.

projects.title: Webserv
projects.summary: A non-blocking HTTP server written from scratch in C++98; I wrote the configuration, GET, POST, DELETE, cookies and sessions.

blocks.html: The second-to-last group project of the core curriculum was to build our own HTTP server.
The server had to:

items: Be configured with a configuration file built from scratch
Be non-blocking
Use a single call to poll
Ensure all reads and writes happen after poll
Avoid directly using errno after a read or write
Handle infinite loops to prevent the server from blocking
Work correctly in a browser
Have error pages
Return correct HTTP status codes
Use CGI
Handle GET, POST, and DELETE methods
Support file uploads
Listen on multiple ports with different content

blocks.html: The mandatory part alone was already a huge undertaking. For the bonuses, we had to manage client sessions and cookies, as well as support multiple CGI types.

My partner took care of the sockets and the poll loop. I wrote the configuration file parsing, with an error message for each malformed directive, the autoindex, the handling of GET, POST and DELETE requests, and the cookies and sessions: each visitor has their own upload folder. We wrote the CGI together.

projects.title: Transcendence
projects.summary: A complete web application built as a team, around Pong; I built the opposing AI and the 3D version of the game.

blocks.html: For this final core curriculum project, which was also a group project, the goal was to build a complete, real-world web application around the game Pong, to be played against an AI or against another player on the same keyboard.
The project had to include:

items: A frontend
A backend
A database

blocks.html: Since many of us were working on it, we also had to maintain clear organisation with clean, readable commits.
The application had to be launchable with a single command inside a container, work correctly in a browser, produce no console errors, and include a privacy policy and terms of use.
On the technical stack side, we needed to:

items: Build a clean, reactive, and responsive frontend
Use a CSS framework
Store sensitive information in a .env file ignored by Git
Create a well-structured database
Implement secure authentication
Validate data on both the frontend and backend
Use HTTPS on the backend

blocks.html: The application relies on React and TypeScript on the client side, and on NestJS microservices on the server side, all in Docker containers.
We could then choose different modules to add to the project.
Some modules were minor and worth one point, while others were major and worth two points.
The goal was to reach 14 points to pass the mandatory part, then 19 points to pass the bonuses.
For my part, I handled two major modules:

items: Building an AI capable of playing Pong against users: it predicts the ball's trajectory, bounces included, only reacts when the ball enters its zone and loses accuracy over a long rally, like a tired player. I made it more human by analysing my own games against it.

Creating a 3D version of Pong with Three.js: models, lighting and palette, a camera that animates during the countdown then orbits the table with the keyboard, and a choice between 2D and 3D with a preview before the game.
